non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Integrated mental health in cardiovascular care
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: i
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Cardiovascular care is optimal if it is person-centred and seeks to improve overall health, not only CV but also mental health, as an integral component.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Integrated mental health in cardiovascular care
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: ii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: A multidisciplinary team including mental health professionals, psychologists, and/or psychiatrists (Psycho-Cardio team) is needed in CV care to provide guidance for practice and appropriate mental health assessment, support, and management to people with CVD and their caregivers.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Integrated mental health in cardiovascular care
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: iii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Cardiovascular services should aspire to implement a Psycho-Cardio team approach, tailored to the local population, context, and resources.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Integrated mental health in cardiovascular care
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: iv
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Implementing the ACTIVE principles is a practical approach to transform routine clinical CV care towards being more person-centred, integrating mental healthcare into routine CV practice to improve care.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Mental health in cardiovascular prevention
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: i
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Management of psychosocial stress and promotion of mental well-being are essential components of integrated CV prevention.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Mental health in cardiovascular prevention
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: ii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Screening for depression, anxiety, and PTSD is advised to be integrated into CV risk assessment.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Mental health conditions in people with established CVD and caregivers
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: i
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: It is reasonable to assess depression, anxiety, and PTSD in people with established CVD as they are highly prevalent and impact outcomes, and refer promptly to a professional when needed.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Mental health conditions in people with established CVD and caregivers
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: ii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Chronic stress and loneliness are associated with negative outcomes in people with CVD and should prompt referral if identified during clinical assessment.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Mental health conditions in people with established CVD and caregivers
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: iii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Incorporating informal caregiver well-being assessment and support is advisable in the holistic approach of mental and CV health.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: i
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Screening of mental health with validated screening tools is advised after a new diagnosis or CV event, at least once during follow-up and anytime based on clinical judgement of need.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: ii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Initial simple screening with a two-item measure (i.e. Whooley questions, PHQ-2, GAD-2) can be incorporated into routine practice.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: iii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: A low threshold for mental health screening in people with CVD is advised, considering the high prevalence of mental health conditions in people with CVD and its impact on outcomes.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: iv
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Following an abnormal result in the initial screening, a longer validated screening instrument should be used to determine if condition severity is low, moderate, or high.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: v
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Psycho-Cardio teams must define who is responsible for the assessment of mental health conditions and how and when it will be done, tailoring it to the specific context and resources.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: vi
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Each Psycho-Cardio team may choose a particular screening tool after careful assessment of its validity, reliability, and applicability to their population, but standardized screening tools are preferred for mental health assessment.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: vii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: People scoring high on a screening questionnaire need referral for diagnostic assessment and appropriate treatment by a mental health professional.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: viii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Applying a stepped care approach to manage mental health conditions in people with CVD is reasonable based on preferences, severity of symptoms and condition, and resources available.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: ix
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Developing and evaluating tailored intervention programmes aimed at alleviating distress of people coping with CVD and caregivers may be useful.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: x
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Lifestyle measures and psycho-education are useful for all people with CVD while psychological therapies may be helpful for people experiencing depression and/or anxiety.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: xi
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Cardiac rehabilitation is an opportunity to screen people for depression and anxiety and can contribute to improve mental health after CV events or be an opportunity to identify and manage mental health conditions.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: xii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Avoiding benzodiazepines as first-line therapy in the management of anxiety and depression is advised.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: xiii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Anxiolytics, sedatives, and hypnotics are overused and overprescribed in the general population, especially among the elderly and people with mental health conditions, so careful selection of indications is advisable.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: xiv
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Antidepressant use is advised for those with moderate to severe anxiety disorders and depression under the guidance of qualified mental health professionals.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: xv
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: The use of antidepressants in HF is only advisable in severe depression symptoms where the risk of untreated depression outweighs the risk of taking antidepressants.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: xvi
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: In people with ventricular arrhythmias, antidepressants associated with an increased propensity to prolong QTc (such as TCAs and possibly citalopram/ escitalopram in dosages over 20 mg), may be switched to newer antidepressants with better safety profiles.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Screening and management of mental health conditions in CVD
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: xvii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Given the frequent interactions between antidepressants and CV drugs affecting their efficacy and safety, therapeutic drug monitoring is advisable to optimize pharmacotherapy and minimize potential side effects and clinically relevant drug interactions.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Severe mental illness and cardiovascular disease
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: i
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Addressing stigma and managing CVD in people with SMI in accordance with CV Guidelines and best clinical practice is a responsibility of all healthcare professionals.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Severe mental illness and cardiovascular disease
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: ii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: CV care for people with SMI can be improved by following a holistic person-centred approach, involving close collaboration between the Psycho-Cardio team with psychiatrists, general practitioners, and sometimes other specialists to proactively facilitate the engagement of people with SMI in such programmes.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Specific populations and modifiers
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: i
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Psycho-Cardio teams may need to tailor their intervention to the specificities of the target population, with special attention to sex differences, age, frailty, and SES.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Specific populations and modifiers
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: ii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: The appropriateness of antidepressants, drug interactions and side effects in the multimorbid, elderly, and frail need careful evaluation by a multidisciplinary team.

non_classified_consensus_statements.specific_topic: Specific populations and modifiers
non_classified_consensus_statements.label: iii
non_classified_consensus_statements.statement: Migrants and refugees may benefit from directed proactive programmes to assess their CV and mental health due to the high prevalence of conditions and their potential difficulties to access the healthcare system.

guideline_updates.old: 2019: SCORE recommended for asymptomatic adults >40 years without CVD, DM, CKD, FH, or LDL-C >4.9 mmol/L (Class I, Level C).
guideline_updates.new: 2025: SCORE2 for apparently healthy people <70 years and SCORE2-OP for those ≥70 years, estimating 10-year fatal and non-fatal CVD risk (both Class I, Level B).
guideline_updates.rationale: The focused update adopts SCORE2/SCORE2-OP to estimate combined fatal and non-fatal CVD risk and aligns risk estimation with newer ESC prevention methodology.

guideline_updates.old: 2019: CAC by CT may be considered as a risk modifier in asymptomatic individuals at low or moderate risk (Class IIb, Level B); carotid/femoral plaque burden should be considered (Class IIa, Level B).
guideline_updates.new: 2025: Subclinical coronary atherosclerosis by imaging or increased CAC should be considered as a risk modifier in moderate-risk individuals or those near treatment thresholds (Class IIa, Level B).
guideline_updates.rationale: Newer data show graded event risk with CAC and improved discrimination/reclassification, including risk associated with non-obstructive coronary plaque.

guideline_updates.old: 2019: Risk modifiers/qualifiers were discussed, but there was no directly matching recommendation in the updated wording.
guideline_updates.new: 2025: Risk modifiers should be considered in moderate-risk individuals or those around treatment decision thresholds (Class IIa, Level B).
guideline_updates.rationale: Population risk models remain relatively crude for individual prediction; the update incorporates modifiers consistent with the 2021 ESC prevention framework.

guideline_updates.old: 2019: Ezetimibe should be considered if a statin regimen is not tolerated (Class IIa, Level C); PCSK9 inhibitor added to ezetimibe may be considered (Class IIb, Level C).
guideline_updates.new: 2025: Non-statin therapies with proven CV benefit are recommended when statins cannot be taken (Class I, Level A); bempedoic acid is recommended to achieve the LDL-C goal (Class I, Level B).
guideline_updates.rationale: CLEAR Outcomes provided cardiovascular outcome evidence for bempedoic acid in statin-intolerant patients.

guideline_updates.area: Bempedoic acid added to background therapy
guideline_updates.new: 2025: Addition of bempedoic acid to maximally tolerated statin with or without ezetimibe should be considered in high- or very-high-risk patients to reach LDL-C goal (Class IIa, Level C).
guideline_updates.rationale: New efficacy and outcome data support bempedoic acid as an additional LDL-C-lowering option.

guideline_updates.new: 2025: Evinacumab should be considered in HoFH patients aged ≥5 years not at LDL-C goal despite maximum lipid-lowering therapy (Class IIa, Level B).
guideline_updates.rationale: Evinacumab trials showed substantial LDL-C lowering in HoFH, including patients with limited response to LDL-receptor-dependent therapies.

guideline_updates.old: 2019: Early high-dose statin was recommended; ezetimibe was added if LDL-C goal remained unmet at 4–6 weeks, and early PCSK9 inhibition was considered mainly when already on maximally tolerated statin plus ezetimibe and above goal.
guideline_updates.new: 2025: Intensify lipid-lowering during the index hospitalization in patients already on therapy (Class I, Level C); consider starting high-intensity statin plus ezetimibe during the index admission in selected treatment-naïve patients (Class IIa, Level B).
guideline_updates.rationale: The update emphasizes the vulnerable early post-ACS period and evidence favoring earlier, stronger LDL-C lowering rather than delayed stepwise escalation.

guideline_updates.old: 2019: Lp(a) measurement should be considered at least once in adulthood to identify very high inherited Lp(a) >180 mg/dL (>430 nmol/L), and in selected patients for risk reclassification (Class IIa, Level C).
guideline_updates.new: 2025: Lp(a) >50 mg/dL (105 nmol/L) should be considered in all adults as a CV risk-enhancing factor, with higher levels conferring progressively greater risk (Class IIa, Level B).
guideline_updates.rationale: The update reflects evidence for a continuous increase in cardiovascular risk across the Lp(a) spectrum and uses >50 mg/dL as a practical risk-enhancing threshold.

guideline_updates.old: 2019: In high-risk or above patients with TG 135–499 mg/dL despite statin therapy, n-3 PUFAs (icosapent ethyl 2 × 2 g/day) should be considered (Class IIa, Level B).
guideline_updates.new: 2025: High-dose icosapent ethyl 2 × 2 g/day should be considered with statin in high- or very-high-risk patients with TG 135–499 mg/dL (Class IIa, Level B).
guideline_updates.rationale: The wording now specifically emphasizes purified high-dose icosapent ethyl after divergent trial results with mixed EPA/DHA preparations such as STRENGTH.

guideline_updates.new: 2025: Volanesorsen 300 mg/week should be considered for severe hypertriglyceridaemia due to FCS to lower triglycerides and reduce pancreatitis risk (Class IIa, Level B).
guideline_updates.rationale: A phase III trial showed marked triglyceride reduction, and pooled randomized data supported reduced acute pancreatitis risk.

guideline_updates.old: 2019: Lipid-lowering therapy, mostly statins, should be considered in HIV patients with dyslipidaemia to achieve the LDL-C goal defined for high-risk patients (Class IIa, Level C).
guideline_updates.new: 2025: Statin therapy is recommended in primary prevention for people with HIV aged ≥40 years irrespective of estimated CV risk and LDL-C level (Class I, Level B), with attention to drug interactions.
guideline_updates.rationale: REPRIEVE showed a 35% lower incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events with pitavastatin versus placebo in people with HIV.

guideline_updates.old: 2019: No specific recommendation in the dyslipidaemia guideline.
guideline_updates.new: 2025: Statins should be considered in adults at high or very high risk of chemotherapy-related CV toxicity to reduce anthracycline-induced cardiac dysfunction (Class IIa, Level B).
guideline_updates.rationale: The recommendation is supported by STOP-CA, other randomized trials/meta-analyses, and is aligned with the 2022 ESC cardio-oncology guideline.

guideline_updates.old: 2019: Healthy diet and selected lipid effects of supplements were discussed; there was no equivalent Class III recommendation against unproven supplements for ASCVD prevention.
guideline_updates.new: 2025: Dietary supplements or vitamins without documented safety and significant LDL-C-lowering efficacy are not recommended to lower ASCVD risk (Class III, Level B).
guideline_updates.rationale: SPORT found no significant LDL-C reduction with tested supplements versus placebo, OMEMI did not reduce clinical events, and clinically relevant outcome evidence remains absent for many supplements.
